propositions.text: The Minister appeals the RPD decision accepting the respondent's refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, (the "appellant") appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) issued on June 24, 2015 with the written Notice of Decision being issued on June 25, 2015, accepting the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "respondent"), a citizen of Libya , for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister appeals the RPD decision accepting the respondent's refugee claim.

propositions.text: The appellant submits new evidence and seeks to have it entered under section 171(a.5) of the Act.
propositions.quote: New evidence has been submitted by the appellant and pursuant to section 171(a.5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act"),1 the appellant seeks to have the new evidence entered in this appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (the "RAD").

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submits new evidence and seeks to have it entered under section 171(a.5) of the Act.

propositions.text: The respondent submits new evidence under sections 110(3) and 110(5) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The respondent has also submitted new evidence pursuant to sections 110(3) and 110(5) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits new evidence under sections 110(3) and 110(5) of the Act.

propositions.text: The appellant does not seek a hearing under section 110(6) of the Act.
propositions.quote: Neither the appellant2 nor the respondent3 seeks a hearing pursuant to section 110(6) of the Act.

propositions.text: The respondent does not seek a hearing under section 110(6) of the Act.
propositions.quote: Neither the appellant2 nor the respondent3 seeks a hearing pursuant to section 110(6) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Neither appellant nor respondent seeks a hearing under section 110(6) of the Act.

propositions.text: The appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and order a re-determination by a different panel.
propositions.quote: The appellant asks the RAD to set aside the determination of the RPD and order the matter be returned to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted Panel.4

paragraphs.summary: The appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and order a re-determination by a different panel.

propositions.text: The respondent asks the RAD to confirm the RPD decision that he is a Convention refugee.
propositions.quote: The respondent asks the RAD to confirm the decision of the RPD that the respondent is a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent asks the RAD to confirm the RPD decision that he is a Convention refugee.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the respondent is a Convention refugee and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the respondent is a Convention refugee. This appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the respondent is a Convention refugee and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: The respondent is a Libyan citizen and small business owner in Libya.
propositions.quote: The respondent is a citizen of Libya. While living in Libya he was a small XXXX XXXX business owner in the city of XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent is a Libyan citizen and small business owner in Libya.

propositions.text: In 2013, the respondent was interviewed expressing negative opinions about religious extremist groups, especially Ansar al-Sharia.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2013 he was interviewed by a XXXX XXXX from the XXXX XXXX "XXXX XXXX" (or XXXX XXXX). During this interview he expressed negative opinions about the state of affairs in Libya focusing specifically on the negative influence of religious extremists groups and singling out the militia group known as Ansar al-Sharia for criticism.

propositions.text: The respondent was excited to express his opinions publicly in the interview.
propositions.quote: The respondent was excited about finally being able to express his opinions in a public forum.

paragraphs.summary: In 2013, the respondent was interviewed expressing negative opinions about religious extremist groups, especially Ansar al-Sharia, and was excited to do so.

propositions.text: The respondent was interviewed in his store by chance; the director was a friend of the respondent.
propositions.quote: The respondent was interviewed in his store. By coincidence the director of this XXXX project was a friend of the respondent, named XXXX XXXX XXXX. The interview had not been pre-arranged and it was only by chance that the respondent was approached to be interviewed for the "man on the street" style interview by Mr. XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent was interviewed in his store by chance; the director was a friend of the respondent.

propositions.text: Another merchant was interviewed expressing similar negative opinions about extremist groups and Ansar al-Sharia.
propositions.quote: A fellow merchant named XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was also interviewed and he too expressed the same type of negative opinions about religious extremist groups in general and Ansar al-Sharia in particular.

propositions.text: The XXXX XXXX in Libya several days after the interviews.
propositions.quote: The XXXX XXXX in Libya several days after the interviews.

paragraphs.summary: Another merchant was interviewed expressing similar negative opinions about extremist groups and Ansar al-Sharia; the XXXX XXXX in Libya several days after.

propositions.text: The respondent received a visitor's visa for Canada in 2013 and travelled to Canada that year.
propositions.quote: Not long after the interview the respondent received a visitor's visa for Canada enabling him to travel to Canada to attend his brother's wedding. The issue date for the visa was XXXX XXXX, 2013 and the expiry date was XXXX XXXX, 2014.5 The respondent travelled to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent received a visitor's visa for Canada in 2013 and travelled to Canada that year.

propositions.text: In 2014, the respondent learned that a friend was murdered by Ansar al-Sharia and that he was threatened and attacked by them.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2014, while still in Canada he received word that XXXX XXXX XXXX had been murdered in XXXX 2014 by members of Ansar al-Sharia. He also learned that one of his employees had been kidnapped and beaten by members of Ansar al-Sharia who had come to his store looking for the respondent. His brother informed him that members of Ansar al-Sharia had come to their house looking for him as well. They apparently threatened to kill him.

paragraphs.summary: In 2014, the respondent learned that a friend was murdered by Ansar al-Sharia and that he was threatened and attacked by them.

propositions.text: Due to threats to his life, the respondent sought refugee protection in Canada in March 2015.
propositions.quote: As a result of the threats to his life the respondent sought refugee protection in Canada on or about March 3, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: Due to threats to his life, the respondent sought refugee protection in Canada in March 2015.

propositions.text: The RAD identifies three issues from the appellant's memo: unreasonableness of RPD findings on threats, faulty IFA analysis, and burden of proof error.
propositions.quote: The appellant has not specifically identified the issues for this appeal under its own heading. The RAD has reviewed the appellant's memo and has identified the following issues in support of his application to have the RAD set aside the RPD decision. 1) Is the RPD decision unreasonable by virtue of not making clear findings on determinative issues in particular the threat to the respondent by Ansar-al-Sharia in XXXX?6 2) Did the RPD conduct a faulty analysis when assessing the suitability of XXXX as an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA).7 3) Did the RPD err in law by shifting the burden of proof from the respondent to the appellant?8 NEW EVIDENCE Appellant

paragraphs.summary: The RAD identifies three issues from the appellant's memo: unreasonableness of RPD findings on threats, faulty IFA analysis, and burden of proof error.

propositions.text: The appellant submits new evidence: a declaration, a death certificate, and a new medical report interpretation.
propositions.quote: The appellant has submitted the following new evidence and seeks to have it entered as evidence in this RAD appeal pursuant to section 171(a.5) of the Act. 1) A Declaration dated August 18, 2015 from CBSA Officer Diana Gunadi;9 2) A copy of a death certificate with the name and pertinent details of the deceased redacted;10 3) A new interpretation of a medical report allegedly issued by the XXXX Hospital in XXXX, Libya and signed by Dr. XXXX XXXX XXXX11 that was entered in evidence at the RPD hearing.12 The new interpretation was completed by Hossein Talebian an accredited translator.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submits new evidence: a declaration, a death certificate, and a new medical report interpretation.

propositions.text: The respondent submits new evidence: an article on Ansar al Sharia and a Canadian government security statement.
propositions.quote: The respondent has submitted the following new evidence and seeks to have it entered as evidence in this RAD appeal pursuant to section 110(3) and 110(5) of the Act:13 4) An article published by The Long War Journal - A Project of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies entitled "Ansar al Sharia Libya fights on under new leader". Published June 30, 2015. 5) Security statement from Government of Canada, "Embassy of Canada to Libya." Last modified June 12, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits new evidence: an article on Ansar al Sharia and a Canadian government security statement.

propositions.text: Neither party made submissions on the standard of review the RAD should apply.
propositions.quote: Neither the appellant nor the respondent made submissions with respect to the standard of review the RAD should apply to the assessment of the RPD decision.

paragraphs.summary: Neither party made submissions on the standard of review the RAD should apply.

propositions.text: The Act does not specify the standard of review for the RAD; courts disagree on it; reasonableness is not appropriate.
propositions.quote: While the Act sets out grounds for appeal, as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the RPD. The first Federal Court (the "Court") review of a RAD decision was in May 2014 (Iyamuremye).14 Since that time there has been a number of Court decisions rendered. It is fair to say that, to a large extent, the Court is not of one mind as to the standard of review that the RAD should apply. The majority of decisions have made one thing clear, however, and that is, the RAD should not apply "reasonableness" as its standard of review. Until such time as the Federal Court of Appeal (the "FCA") brings more clarity to the standard of review I take the Court's direction on this issue and do not apply the standard of reasonableness to this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Act does not specify the standard of review for the RAD; courts disagree on it; reasonableness is not appropriate.

propositions.text: The RAD must comprehensively review evidence and substitute its own determination if it departs from the RPD's findings.
propositions.quote: I have examined the various Court decisions regarding the role of the RAD and find that the process of a hybrid appeal proposed by Mr. Justice Phelan in Huruglica15 is consistent with the common thread found in the majority of the Court decisions that state the RAD must comprehensively review the available relevant evidence when assessing the RPD's findings and come to an assessment of the appellant's refugee claim. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD must comprehensively review evidence and substitute its own determination if it departs from the RPD's findings.

propositions.text: RAD can respect RPD's credibility conclusions and advantages in fact-finding
propositions.quote: Mr. Justice Phelan determined that, in conducting its assessment, the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion.

propositions.text: RAD is not restricted to intervening on facts only for palpable and overriding error like an appellate court
propositions.quote: The RAD is, however, not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on the facts only where there is "palpable and overriding error".

paragraphs.summary: Prior court held RAD can respect RPD credibility findings but is not limited to intervening only for palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: I reviewed all evidence in the RPD Record and conducted my own independent assessment
propositions.quote: I undertook to examine and review all the evidence in the RPD Record (RPDR) and, unless otherwise stated, conducted my own independent assessment of the evidence and came to my own conclusion based on that evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court independently reviewed all evidence in the RPD record and made its own conclusions.

propositions.text: Section 110(3) allows RAD to accept documentary evidence and written submissions from Minister and appellant
propositions.quote: Section 110(3) of the Act, states the RAD may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and the person who is subject of the appeal.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) restricts appellant to evidence arising after claim rejection or not reasonably available before
propositions.quote: Section 110(4) of the Act directs that the person subject of the appeal may only present evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or evidence that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of rejection.

propositions.text: Section 110(5) excludes application of section 110(4) to evidence responding to Minister's evidence
propositions.quote: Section 110(5) states that this section does not apply in respect of evidence that is presented in response to evidence presented by the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains statutory provisions governing RAD's acceptance of evidence and appellant's limitations on new evidence.

propositions.text: Section 171(a.5) allows Minister to submit documentary evidence and written submissions anytime before RAD decision
propositions.quote: Section 171(a.5) states that the Minister may submit documentary evidence and make written submissions in support of the Minister's appeal at any time before the RAD makes a decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Minister may submit evidence anytime before RAD decision under section 171(a.5).

propositions.text: Madam Justice Gagné found section 110(4) must be applied flexibly to not hinder full fact-based appeal
propositions.quote: Madam Justice Gagné found in the matter of Singh16 that section 110(4) of the Act must be applied by the RAD with sufficient flexibility so as not to hinder the full fact-based appeal the RAD is mandated to conduct.

propositions.text: Mr. Justice Barnes strongly endorsed Gagné's finding in Sow
propositions.quote: Mr. Justice Barnes strongly endorsed this finding in Sow.17

paragraphs.summary: Prior judges found section 110(4) must be applied flexibly to allow full fact-based appeals.

propositions.text: Madam Justice Strickland found RAD has no discretion to refuse evidence meeting section 110(4) requirements
propositions.quote: Madam Justice Strickland recently found in the matter of Deri:18 [60] By contrast, s. 110(4) offers the RAD no discretion to refuse to apply its explicit admissibility requirements for new evidence.

propositions.text: If new evidence meets s.110(4) requirements, RAD must accept it; if not, must reject it
propositions.quote: If the new evidence meets the requirements of s. 110(4) then the RAD must accept it. Conversely, if it does not, then the RAD must reject it.

propositions.text: Assessment of reasonable availability is factual but does not change ultimate admissibility decision
propositions.quote: While there is an element of subjectivity in assessing whether the evidence was reasonably available or if an applicant could not reasonably been expected to have previously presented it, this is a factual assessment, it does not alter the character of the ultimate decision as to admissibility.

propositions.text: Strickland found RAD's interpretation of s.110(4) reasonable
propositions.quote: Accordingly, in my view, the RAD's interpretation of s. 110(4) was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Madam Justice Strickland held RAD must accept evidence meeting s.110(4) criteria; assessment is factual and interpretation reasonable.

propositions.text: Many RAD Members apply Raza criteria for new evidence acceptance
propositions.quote: Many RAD Members have applied the criteria as set out in Raza19 as the standard for the acceptance of new evidence.

propositions.text: Court has found Raza factors do not apply to RAD as appeal division
propositions.quote: The Court has, in some of their reviews of the RAD decisions, determined that the factors set out in the Raza decision do not apply to the RAD in its capacity of an appeal division.

paragraphs.summary: RAD members often apply Raza criteria, but court has found these do not apply to RAD appeals.

propositions.text: Raza dealt with PRRA but uses same legal test as s.110(4)
propositions.quote: Raza dealt with a pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA) but the wording in the legislation enshrines the same legal test as set out in section 110(4).

propositions.text: FCA identified credibility, newness, relevance, materiality as factors in Raza
propositions.quote: In Raza the FCA identified credibility, newness, relevance, and materiality as issues to be considered.

propositions.text: Court opinions differ on applying Raza to RAD appeals
propositions.quote: As with the RAD standard of review issue, there is no comity within the Court regarding following the jurisprudence as set out in Raza.

propositions.text: Justice Mosley disagreed with reservations about applying Raza to RAD appeals in Denbel
propositions.quote: Mr. Justice Mosley stated in Denbel:20 [42] In Khachatourian above21 at para 37, Justice Simon Noël expressed reservations about the propriety of transposing Raza to the RAD context, referring to the analysis of Justice Gagné in Singh v. Canada. . . . Once again I respectfully disagree. . . .

propositions.text: Parliament intended s.110(4) and PRRA provisions to enshrine same legal test
propositions.quote: In my view, Parliament intended these two provisions to enshrine the same legal test.

propositions.text: If Parliament intended more flexible RAD admissibility rules, it would not have replicated restrictive PRRA language
propositions.quote: If Parliament had intended to establish more flexible admissibility rules in RAD appeals, it would not have replicated the restrictive language which governs PRRAs.

paragraphs.summary: Raza applies same legal test as s.110(4); courts differ on applying Raza to RAD appeals; some judges say Parliament intended same test.

propositions.text: Conflicting binding findings place RAD members in a dilemma
propositions.quote: Competing findings such as those identified above, all binding on the RAD, place RAD Members on the "horns of a dilemma."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds conflicting binding precedents place RAD members in a dilemma.

propositions.text: Until FCA clarifies, I will apply s.110(4) and RAD Rules with flexibility and consider if excluding evidence hinders full fact-based review
propositions.quote: Until such time as the FCA brings clarity to this issue, when applying the conditions for new evidence as set out in section 110(4) of the Act and section 29(4) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (the "RAD Rules"),22 I will consider whether exclusion of the proposed evidence would hinder a full fact based review of the appeal and at the same time will respect and apply the legislation that governs the acceptance of new evidence.

propositions.text: I will use Raza factors as a flexible guide for new evidence acceptance
propositions.quote: The factors as identified in Raza will be used as a guide and will be applied with flexibility.

propositions.text: Properly applied, Raza principles and statutory conditions are not mutually exclusive
propositions.quote: If applied properly I do not find these guiding principles to be mutually exclusive.

paragraphs.summary: The court will flexibly apply s.110(4) and RAD Rules, using Raza factors as guide, until FCA clarifies.

propositions.text: Minister's documentary evidence normally requires no analysis due to section 171(a.5) authority
propositions.quote: Under normal circumstances there would be no analysis required for documents entered by the Minister as section 171(a.5) gives the Minister statutory authority to enter documentary evidence at any time before the RAD renders its decision.

propositions.text: This case is unique and requires analysis of Officer Gunadi's declaration as new evidence
propositions.quote: This matter, however, is unique and an analysis of the declaration of Officer Gunadi, which is put forward by the Minister as new evidence, is required.

paragraphs.summary: Normally Minister's evidence needs no analysis, but Officer Gunadi's declaration requires special analysis here.

propositions.text: Officer Gunadi's declaration does not state Mr. Talebian was interpreter but RPDR shows he was
propositions.quote: In her declaration Officer Gunadi does not specifically state that Mr. Talebian was the interpreter for the respondent's RPD hearing but does make reference to him reviewing the medical report at the hearing. The RPDR clearly establishes that Mr. Talebian was the interpreter at the respondent's RPD hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Officer Gunadi's declaration omits interpreter role, but RPDR confirms Mr. Talebian was interpreter at RPD hearing.

propositions.text: Officer Gunadi states Mr. Talebian said medical report was poorly written and inconsistent with past documents
propositions.quote: Officer Gunadi states in her declaration that Mr. Talebain advised her that the medical report was poorly written and not consistent with medical documents he had interpreted in the past.

propositions.text: Mr. Talebian opined it was odd for doctor to include Ansar al-Sharia info in medical report
propositions.quote: He also offered his opinion that it is odd that a doctor would include information pertaining to Ansar al-Sharia as normally medical reports only includes medical information.

paragraphs.summary: Officer Gunadi reports Mr. Talebian criticized medical report's quality and content as unusual.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed RPD audio recording showing interpreter's comments about medical report during break
propositions.quote: The RAD reviewed the audio recording of the RPD hearing and noted that the RPD adjourned for what the Member described as a five minute break23 but did not turn off the recording.

propositions.text: Interpreter told Minister's representative medical document was poorly written and not by educated person
propositions.quote: Mr. Talebain can be heard telling the Minister's representative that the medical document is poorly written and not the writing of an educated person.

propositions.text: Officer Gunadi references this conversation in her declaration
propositions.quote: Officer Gunadi also makes reference to this conversation in her declaration.

paragraphs.summary: RAD heard interpreter criticize medical report during recorded break; Officer Gunadi referenced this in her declaration.

propositions.text: Minister's section 171(a.5) authority to submit evidence is not absolute
propositions.quote: The Minister is given statutory authority by virtue of section 171(a.5) to submit documentary evidence or make written submissions at any time before the RAD has rendered it's decision, this authorization, however, is not absolute.

propositions.text: Interpreter abandoned impartial duty by giving opinion on medical report authenticity
propositions.quote: The content of this document leads the RAD to conclude that the interpreter abandoned his duty to be impartial.

propositions.text: Interpreter's role is to interpret accurately, not to give evidence or conclusions before RPD or counsel
propositions.quote: The interpreter's role in the hearing is to interpret accurately, to the best of his ability. He is not to give evidence or offer his conclusions of the evidence either before the RPD or in private to counsel.

paragraphs.summary: Minister's authority to submit evidence is limited; interpreter gave opinion breaching impartiality and role.

propositions.text: Interpreter's actions may have violated IRB Code of Conduct for interpreters
propositions.quote: The actions of the interpreter may have violated Immigration and Refugee Board (the "IRB") Code of Conduct for interpreters when he offered his unsolicited opinion regarding the authenticity of the medical report, to Minister's counsel.

propositions.text: IRB Code requires interpreters to be objective and impartial at all times
propositions.quote: Interpreter Service Contractors shall be, and shall appear to be, objective and impartial at all times, inside or outside the conference or hearing room, in relation to any matter for which they provide services to the Board.

paragraphs.summary: Interpreter's unsolicited opinion may violate IRB Code requiring interpreters to be objective and impartial.

propositions.text: Minister's counsel acted inappropriately by listening to and not disclosing interpreter's opinion to parties
propositions.quote: It was also not appropriate for Minister's counsel, firstly, to have listened to the interpreter give his opinion and once having heard him not to have revealed the conversation to the Presiding Member and Counsel for the respondent.

propositions.text: Minister's counsel must follow proper procedure and not use interpreter as evidence against respondent
propositions.quote: It is not appropriate to use the individual who interpreted in the respondent's hearing to give evidence in an adversarial process in support of the Minister's appeal which argues against the positive determination of the RPD.

propositions.text: Minister's counsel placed interpreter in position risking IRB Code violation by cooperating with Minister
propositions.quote: In doing so the Minister's representative was placing the interpreter in a position where, if he co-operates with the Minister, he could be violating the IRB Code of Conduct.

paragraphs.summary: Minister's counsel improperly used interpreter's opinion as evidence, risking Code violation and breaching procedure.

propositions.text: Respondent has right to impartial interpreter adhering to IRB Code of Conduct
propositions.quote: The respondent has the right to expect that the interpreter will be impartial and not act as an agent for the Minister. The respondent further has the right to expect that the interpreter will adhere to the Code of Conduct of the IRB.

propositions.text: RAD must determine if evidence tainted by circumstances violates respondent's right to fundamental justice and fairness
propositions.quote: it is the responsibility of this RAD to determine if the proposed evidence is so tainted by the circumstances leading up to the appellant obtaining it, that the respondent's right to fundamental justice and procedural fairness would be violated if the appellant's exhibit No. 1 is accepted as evidence in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent has right to impartial interpreter; RAD must assess if evidence tainted by circumstances violates fairness rights.

propositions.text: There was breach of procedural fairness or natural justice in how evidence was obtained and interpreter gave evidence discrediting respondent
propositions.quote: Having carefully considered the facts surrounding the appellant obtaining the evidence contained in Officer Gunadi's declaration I find that there was a breach in procedural fairness and/or natural justice in the manner the evidence was obtained and the fact that the interrupter at the RPD hearing was the same person giving the evidence which is meant to discredit the respondent.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds breach of procedural fairness in how evidence was obtained and interpreter gave evidence against respondent.

propositions.text: Court upheld RAD decision excluding evidence obtained after procedural fairness breach in Gutierrez
propositions.quote: The Court recently dealt with a similar issue in the matter of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v. Paramo de Gutierrez.27 In Gutierrez the Court upheld a RAD decision that CBSA breached procedural fairness by not respecting Mr. Gutierrez's right to counsel. The Court also upheld the RAD finding that the RPD breached procedural fairness when it did not exclude evidence obtained by CBSA after the breach.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Gutierrez where RAD excluded evidence obtained after procedural fairness breach.

propositions.text: The RAD found the Minister breached procedural fairness by using the same interpreter to discredit the respondent.
propositions.quote: this RAD has determined that the Minister breached procedural fairness by using the interpreter who was utilized during the RPD hearing, to obtain evidence that is intended to be used to discredit the respondent.

propositions.text: Jurisprudence and natural justice require excluding evidence obtained from that breach.
propositions.quote: The jurisprudence and natural justice dictate that the RAD would err if it did not exclude the evidence obtained as a result of that breach.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Minister breached procedural fairness by using the same interpreter to discredit the respondent and must exclude that evidence.

propositions.text: Accepting appellant's new evidence No. 1 would breach fundamental justice and procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: I find that should the appellant's new evidence no.1 be accepted in this appeal it would amount to a breach of fundamental justice and/or procedural fairness.

propositions.text: The RAD rejects the appellant's new evidence No. 1 despite section 171(a.5) of the Act.
propositions.quote: the RAD rejects the new evidence No. 1 in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejects appellant's new evidence No. 1 as it breaches fundamental justice and procedural fairness.

propositions.text: The RAD accepts new evidence No. 2 and No. 3 under section 171(a.5) of the Act.
propositions.quote: New evidence No. 2 and No. 3 are accepted pursuant to section 171(a.5) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD accepts new evidence No. 2 and No. 3 under the Act.

propositions.text: Respondent's new evidence No. 4 and No. 5 are accepted under section 110(5) of the Act as response to appellant's new evidence.
propositions.quote: therefore pursuant to section 110(5) of the Act the respondent's new evidence No. 4 and No. 5 are accepted for this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD accepts respondent's new evidence No. 4 and No. 5 as response to appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: Section 110(3) directs RAD to proceed without hearing based on RPD record, with exceptions.
propositions.quote: Section 110(3) of the Act directs the RAD, with certain exceptions, to proceed without a hearing on the basis of the record of proceedings from the RPD.

propositions.text: Section 110(6) allows RAD to hold hearing if documentary evidence raises serious credibility issue, is central, and justifies allowing or rejecting claim.
propositions.quote: Section 110(6) states the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, the documentary evidence referred to in section (3): a. raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is subject of the appeal; b. is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim and, c. if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The Act directs RAD to proceed without hearing unless evidence raises serious credibility issues central to the claim and justifies allowing or rejecting it.

propositions.text: Neither party requested a hearing in this matter.
propositions.quote: Neither party has requested a hearing in this matter.

propositions.text: New evidence accepted deals with credibility but alone does not justify allowing or rejecting claim.
propositions.quote: The new evidence accepted in this appeal does deal with credibility but forms only part of the evidence that would be considered in an overall credibility assessment and therefore, in and by itself, would not justify allowing or rejecting the claim.

paragraphs.summary: No hearing requested; new evidence relates to credibility but alone insufficient to decide claim.

propositions.text: No hearing will be ordered in this matter.
propositions.quote: No hearing will be ordered in this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will not order a hearing in this matter.

propositions.text: The RPD decision is unreasonable for lacking clear findings and sufficient analysis on Ansar al-Sharia threat in Tripoli.
propositions.quote: The appellant states that the RPD decision is unreasonable as it does not make clear findings on issues or provide sufficient analysis when assessing the threat of Ansar al-Sharia to the respondent in XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD decision is unreasonable for unclear findings on Ansar al-Sharia threat.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in fact by relying on outdated UK Home Office guidance instead of newer appellant evidence.
propositions.quote: the appellant states the RPD erred in fact when it relied on the information contained in the United Kingdom Home Office Operational Guidance note published in May 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred by relying on outdated UK guidance instead of newer evidence.

propositions.text: Newer document shows Ansar al-Sharia's power fading and joining other groups; RPD erred concluding group was expanding.
propositions.quote: The information the appellant submits that is contained in the newer document and not in the Home Office report, is that the power and influence of Ansar al-Sharia was fading and in order to survive have joined other Islamic groups, and that the RPD erred when it concluded that the group was expanding by virtue of mergers with these other fundamental Islamic factions.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues newer evidence shows Ansar al-Sharia fading and RPD erred concluding expansion.

propositions.text: The RPD used the Zelin article to find Ansar al-Sharia joined other factions under MSTB and is not restricted to certain areas.
propositions.quote: I note that it used information from the Zelin article to conclude that Ansar al-Sharia had joined forces with other Islamic factions under the banner of Majlis Shura Thuwar Benghazi (MSTB, the Benghazi Revolutionaries Consultative Council).

propositions.text: Evidence does not establish MSTB or Ansar al-Sharia is restricted from areas like Tripoli.
propositions.quote: The evidence does not establish that MSTB and/or Ansar al-Sharia is restricted to certain areas of Libya, nor does it establish that areas of operation such as Tripoli are out of reach for them.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds RPD correctly used Zelin article showing Ansar al-Sharia joined MSTB and is not restricted from Tripoli.

propositions.text: Zelin article does not establish Ansar al-Sharia is no longer a threat in Tripoli; MSTB remains potent.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with the appellant that the Zelin article establishes on the balance of probabilities that Ansar al-Sharia is no longer a threat to the respondent in Tripoli.

propositions.text: Article states it is uncertain if Ansar al-Sharia will maintain independence or sustain operations beyond Benghazi.
propositions.quote: One of those issues is whether or not Ansar al-Sharia will maintain its independence or slowly merge with the other military outfits.

propositions.text: Article states it remains to be seen if Ansar al-Sharia can operate in cities beyond Benghazi, not that it cannot.
propositions.quote: The article also states it remains to be seen if Ansar al-Sharia can sustain operations in cities beyond its Benghazi base.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Zelin article does not prove Ansar al-Sharia is no longer a threat or restricted to Benghazi.

propositions.text: Appellant's own evidence does not support that Ansar al-Sharia is no longer a serious threat in Tripoli or Libya.
propositions.quote: This is the appellant's own evidence and to suggest that it establishes that Ansar al Sharia is no longer a serious threat to the respondent in Tripoli, or any other part of Libya for that matter, is not supported by this evidence or other evidence entered at the RPD hearing or this RAD appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds appellant's evidence does not support that Ansar al-Sharia is no longer a serious threat in Libya.

propositions.text: Insufficient credible evidence that Ansar al-Sharia lost influence by merger; merger may have strengthened group.
propositions.quote: There is insufficient credible evidence before me to find that Ansar al-Sharia has lost its influence by virtue of the merger.

propositions.text: RPD concluded merger strengthened group; appellant disagrees but no error in fact found.
propositions.quote: This is the conclusion that the RPD came to after it assessed the evidence, a conclusion the appellant obviously disagrees with but that does make it an error in fact.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no credible evidence Ansar al-Sharia lost influence; merger may have strengthened it, supporting RPD's conclusion.

propositions.text: Respondent's new evidence No. 4 shows Ansar al-Sharia remains active and unrestricted in Libya.
propositions.quote: The inescapable conclusion after reviewing this evidence is that Ansar al-Sharia is still very active in Libya and is not restricted from operating in any particular area of Libya.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent's new evidence No. 4 confirms Ansar al-Sharia remains active and unrestricted in Libya.

propositions.text: RAD concurs with RPD that Ansar al-Sharia poses threat throughout Libya and respondent faces persecution risk everywhere.
propositions.quote: this RAD concurs with the RPD finding regarding the threat that Answar al-Sharia poses to the respondent in every part of Libya and finds that there is more than a reasonable chance that the respondent would face persecution in all parts of Libya.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with RPD that Ansar al-Sharia threatens the respondent throughout Libya, risking persecution everywhere.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges RPD erred by ignoring respondent's viva voce evidence and death certificate evidence.
propositions.quote: The appellant states the RPD erred in fact by ignoring the viva voce evidence of the respondent and the evidence contained in the National Documentation Package regarding the issuance of a death certificate and a burial permit.

propositions.text: Appellant's allegation relates to credibility as RPD addressed it under 'Credibility Concerns'.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the appellant is identifying this to the RAD in an effort to establish the respondent was not credible regarding his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleges RPD ignored evidence affecting credibility; RAD finds this relates to credibility issues addressed by RPD.

propositions.text: Appellant submits witness and respondent were inconsistent about how they first met.
propositions.quote: The appellant also submits that the witness, Mr. Sanussi, and the respondent were not consistent regarding their evidence as to how they first met.

propositions.text: RPD acknowledged inconsistency but found it not unusual for friends to forget how they met.
propositions.quote: The RPD acknowledged this inconsistency but concluded that it was not unusual for two men who frequented the same social circle to forget where and how they first met.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleges inconsistency in witness and respondent evidence; RPD found this inconsistency not unusual.

propositions.text: Court finds RAD can respect RPD's credibility conclusions where RPD has advantage.
propositions.quote: In keeping with the Court's finding I take notice that the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds RAD can respect RPD's credibility conclusions where RPD has advantage.

propositions.text: RPD is best positioned to assess credibility as it observed and questioned appellant on credibility issues.
propositions.quote: It is the RPD that is in the best position to make a finding on credibility as it was the RPD who had the appellant before it and was able to observe the appellant and question him on credibility related issues.

propositions.text: This is the only deference RAD affords the RPD in this appeal.
propositions.quote: This is the only deference I afford the RPD regarding this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD defers to RPD's credibility findings as RPD was best placed to assess appellant's credibility.

propositions.text: Analyzing findings of fact and credibility determinations fall within the RPD's expertise
propositions.quote: The Court has stated that analyzing findings of fact and determinations of credibility fall within the heartland of the RPD expertise.38

paragraphs.summary: The Court states that analyzing findings of fact and credibility determinations is within the RPD's expertise.

propositions.text: RPD did not ignore documentary evidence about death and burial certificates despite not dealing with it specifically
propositions.quote: Although it would have been preferable if the RPD dealt specifically with the documentary evidence in the NDP regarding the issuing of death and burial certificates as it related to the matter before it, I find that the RPD did not ignore the evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent was questioned about discrepancies in documentary evidence and stated he did not know reasons for date or issuing authority differences
propositions.quote: The respondent was questioned on it and stated that he simply did not know why the issuance date on the evidence was not the same as the date of death. He also testified that he had no knowledge as to why there would be two different issuing authorities on the document, one from the Ministry of Defense and one from the Ministry of Health.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not ignore documentary evidence; the respondent was questioned and said he did not know about discrepancies.

propositions.text: RPD explained the weight it placed on discrepancies and found them unpersuasive to challenge respondent's credibility
propositions.quote: The RPD dealt with the weight it placed on these discrepancies in its Reasons. It is not necessary for me to restate in different words what the RPD adequately explained in its decision.39 The RPD clearly set out what inconsistencies it was concerned with and why it did not find them to be persuasive in challenging the respondent's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD adequately explained why discrepancies did not undermine respondent's credibility.

propositions.text: RPD decision is logical, based on evidence, consistent with jurisprudence, and credibility finding is deferred to RPD
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the entire record and find the RPD decision to be logical, solidly based on the evidence before it and in keeping with existing jurisprudence. I defer to the RPD regarding its finding regarding the credibility of the respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD decision logical, evidence-based, consistent with law, and defers to RPD on credibility.

propositions.text: Whether the RPD shifted the burden of proof onto the Minister as argued by the appellant
propositions.quote: The appellant argues that the RPD shifted this burden onto the Minister and identifies language used by the RPD in its Reasons in support of this argument.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD shifted burden of proof to the Minister, raising this issue for decision.

propositions.text: Use of phrase 'the Minister has not established' is unfortunate but does not prove burden shift to Minister
propositions.quote: It is unfortunate that the words "the Minister has not established" are used in the RPD Reasons as these words are open to misinterpretation. I do not agree, however, that the use of these words establishes that the RPD shifted the burden of proof to the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the phrase 'the Minister has not established' is unfortunate but does not show burden shift to Minister.

propositions.text: RPD has expertise and would know to apply the burden of proof correctly
propositions.quote: The RAD recognizes the level of expertise that the RPD has. It is incomprehensible to this RAD that the RPD would not know and apply such a basic principle as the burden of proof to its decision making.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it incomprehensible that the RPD would misapply the burden of proof given its expertise.

propositions.text: RPD meant appellant made no submissions on state protection or IFA, a legitimate consideration, not burden shift
propositions.quote: The appellant has misinterpreted the meaning of these words in the context of the RPD decision. This RAD concludes that the RPD is stating that the appellant made no submissions regarding state protection or internal flight alternative (IFA) inferring that if there was a viable IFA and/or adequate state protection available the appellant would have made submissions in this regard. This is a legitimate consideration when addressing these two issues.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD was noting appellant's lack of submissions on state protection or IFA, not shifting burden.

propositions.text: Minister's representative told RPD state protection was not an issue at hearing
propositions.quote: This RAD notes that the Minister's representative advised the RPD that in his opinion state protection was not an issue at the refugee protection hearing.40

propositions.text: Appellant cannot claim prejudice from alleged wrong standard on issue he said was irrelevant
propositions.quote: It is difficult for the appellant to now argue that he has somehow been prejudiced by the RPD applying the wrong standard of review on an issue that he determined was not relevant in the refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Minister said state protection was not an issue and appellant cannot claim prejudice from alleged wrong standard on that issue.

propositions.text: Phrase 'Minister has not established lack of subjective fear' is unfortunate but does not show burden shift
propositions.quote: The appellant further submits that the RPD stated that the Minister has not established a lack of subjective fear. Once again, I find the wording to be unfortunate but do not agree with the appellant that it indicates that the RPD was shifting the burden of proof to the Minister.

propositions.text: RPD analyzed subjective fear in light of Minister's submissions and found them unpersuasive, proper decision making
propositions.quote: Examining this statement in the context of the entire set of Reasons, this RAD concludes that the RPD was analyzing the issue of subjective fear in light of the Minister's submission. What the RPD is saying is that the Minister's arguments were not persuasive enough to move the RPD from its determination that the respondent did establish a subjective fear at his RPD hearing. This is within the mandate of the RPD and totally proper in the decision making process.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the phrase about Minister not establishing lack of fear is unfortunate but shows proper analysis, not burden shift.

propositions.text: RAD confirms the RPD decision for the reasons given
propositions.quote: For the above reasons the RAD confirms the RPD decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision for the reasons stated.

propositions.text: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, RAD confirms RPD decision that respondent is a Convention Refugee and dismisses appeal
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the respondent is a Convention Refugee. This appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision that respondent is a Convention Refugee and dismisses the appeal.
